result.final_text:
## What this letter says
Your doctor wrote to another doctor. The letter tells that doctor about you.
You have Wilson's disease. You were told this at age 14. You take penicillamine.
You had short breath, a fast heartbeat (palpitations) and chest discomfort. Doctors found atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate. You stayed in hospital and were watched.
Your heart went back to normal sinus rhythm by itself. You needed no more treatment.
An echocardiogram showed mild-to-moderate left atrial enlargement. Your ejection fraction was normal. There was no other significant valve problem.
Doctors in North Carolina were worried about cirrhosis. You have never had a liver biopsy. So this diagnosis is in doubt. Your liver status is not clear.
Your liver tests (LFTs) stayed normal. Your copper level is undetectable on your penicillamine dose.
Your rhythm was normal when your doctor saw you. You take metoprolol and aspirin with no trouble.
Your atrial fibrillation may come and go (paroxysmal). This is only possible.
Coumadin was not started. Liver doctors said to avoid it. They said your liver disease is questionable but significant.
Your doctor asks the new doctor for advice. It is about long-term anticoagulation and rhythm control.

## What you need to do
1. Go to your visit with the new doctor. You will be seen soon.
2. Keep taking your medicines as you do now. The letter says to continue all three.
3. Do not start Coumadin on your own. It was not started.

## Dates and medicines
Date: 06/12/2008. Your doctor saw you then. Your rhythm was normal. The letter does not say if this is 6 December or 12 June.

Medicines:
- Penicillamine: 250 milligrams, by mouth, four times a day. Continue.
- Metoprolol (Lopressor): 12.5 milligrams, twice a day. Continue. It was started at the North Carolina hospital. You do well on it.
- Aspirin: 325 milligrams, once a day. Continue. It was started instead of Coumadin. This was due to the questionable significant liver disease.

## Questions to ask your doctor
- What are my options for long-term anticoagulation?
- What are my options for rhythm control?
- How can we learn more about my liver?

## When to get urgent help
The letter does not list specific warning signs.

If you are worried and it is not an emergency, call NHS 111. In an emergency, call 999.

---
